newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Le Pen calls Bosnian Serb nationalists "patriots".
newsitem.headline: Le Pen calls Bosnian Serb nationalists "patriots".

text.p: French far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen hailed ultra-nationalist leaders of Bosnia's Serb republic as fellow "patriots" on Thursday, saying they were misunderstood.
Le Pen was treated as an honoured guest by his hosts in the Serb government seat of Pale, a mountain village outside the Bosnian capital Sarajevo.
"I wish to convey to your people greetings from French patriots," Le Pen told the Serb member of Bosnia's collective presidency, Momcilo Krajisnik, upon arrival.
After more than an hour of talks with Krajisnik and other Serb political leaders, Le Pen told reporters the foreign media had demonised the Bosnian Serbs in the Yugoslav conflict.

"We are not among those who blindly believe what they have been told. We have had an opportunity to see for ourselves and in other circumstances how much opinion has been manipulated and how much the reality was different from what the media had shown us," Le Pen said.
"I believe that, like others, they (Serbs) suffered in the recent war as well."
Krajisnik welcomed the comments, saying: "Your words are like a remedy for the soul and we understand them completely."
During Bosnia's 3-1/2 year war, Western governments condemned the separatist Serb leadership for conducting a campaign of expulsions against Moslems and Croats and for the brutal siege of Sarajevo.
The same Serb leadership had their army fire on French U.N. peacekeeping soldiers during the war and took them hostage to prevent allied air strikes.
Yet Le Pen had nothing but generous words for the Serb authorities in Pale. His three-day visit was organised by the hardline nationalist Serbian Radical Party in neighbouring Yugoslavia.

Le Pen said he wished to restore a "traditional alliance" between France and Serbs dating back to World War I. "This (French-Serb) alliance has been covered by a cloud and I hope it won't return ever again," he said.

Le Pen, who was scheduled to spend the night in nearby Sokolac in Serb-controlled territory, also criticised the French role in NATO bombing raids against Bosnian Serb targets at the close of the war.
"I told my counterparts that the French people had no part in the decision to pursue military aggression against the Serbs," he said.
The National Front leader and the Serb nationalists share a hostility towards co-existence with Moslems of any nationality.
Le Pen has led his National Front party to prominence by playing to anti-immigrant sentiment in France, winning votes with tirades against Arab immigrants from former North African colonies.

Le Pen had lunch with Bosnian Serb political leaders at presidential offices in Pale. Located in the grounds of a diesel engine factory, it is the headquarters of wartime Bosnian Serb president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
There was no official confirmation whether Karadzic, who still wields political power behind the scenes despite giving up the post of president, dined with Le Pen.
But Karadzic, who has refused to face war crimes charges before a U.N. tribunal, is known to receive visitors at his office in the heavily-guarded headquarters.
Le Pen's visit sparked controversy at home in the ranks of his own party, where pro-Croatian sympathisers are particularly powerful.

The daily newspaper Present, voice of ultra-traditionalist Catholics in the FN, wrote last week that "simpletons in our own political family who try to pass off the killer Seselj as a so-called nationalist opponent to the "Serbolshevik' Milosevic demonstrate their complete ignorance of the situation."
Le Pen visited the Serbian capital Belgrade on Tuesday accompanied by Radical party leader Vojislav Seselj, once a close ally of Serbia's Socialist President Slobodan Milosevic.
